options: An expression that evaluates to TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN — the general mechanism SQL Server uses to filter data
Another name for a column alias
A synonym for a stored procedure
questions.explain: Every condition you write in WHERE (and elsewhere) is a predicate, resolving to one of these three states for each row.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a predicate from this chapter?
questions.explain: ListPrice > 100 evaluates to TRUE or FALSE per row — a classic comparison predicate.

questions.q: Besides WHERE, where else have you already used predicates in this course?
options: Predicates only ever appear in WHERE
Inside a searched CASE expression's WHEN clauses
questions.explain: Chapter 1's searched CASE (Lesson 8) used full boolean conditions in each WHEN — those are predicates too.

questions.q: Which value can a predicate resolve to, in addition to TRUE and FALSE?
options: UNKNOWN — the special result NULL comparisons produce
questions.explain: This ties back to Lesson 16 — a comparison involving NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE or FALSE.

questions.q: Which upcoming clause (covered starting in Chapter 3) also expects a predicate?
options: The semicolon at the end of a statement
questions.explain: A JOIN's ON condition works exactly like a WHERE condition — it's a predicate that determines which row combinations match.
